newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Chechnya's hero Maskhadov to run for president.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya's hero Maskhadov to run for president.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov, chief commander of Chechnya's independence fighters who have humiliated the Russian army, said on Tuesday he planned to run in the presidential election expected early next year.
"I have decided I will be a candidate," Maskhadov, who now heads the Chechen government effectively recognised by Moscow, told reporters outside his office in central Grozny.
Maskhadov's announcement ends weeks of speculation about whether or not he planned to seek office.
Current leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and guerrilla chief Shamil Basayev have already thrown their hats into the ring, but observers see Maskhadov as a strong early favorite.
Moscow's battered troops are in the final stages of a humiliating retreat from the mountainous Caucasus region along its southern border with Georgia.
They failed to crush rebel resistance in 21 months of war which killed tens of thousands of people.

Russian human rights campaigner Sergei Kovalyov told separatist leaders last week the vote risked being turned into a farce unless it was postponed to give time to establish valid voting rules and find ways for an estimated 400,000 refugees -- nearly half the population -- who fled the war, to cast ballots.
But Maskhadov gave no indication the January 27 poll, which will also choose a local parliament, would be delayed.
"We need to hold elections quickly," he said, clad in a traditional Chechen lambswool hat and flanked by armed bodyguards.
Some pro-independence politicians have suggested that separatists rally around a single candidate, most likely Maskhadov, with others withdrawing in a show of unity.
But the deceptively soft-spoken former Soviet army colonel said giving voters too few choices risked destroying the legitimacy of the elections.
"When there is one candidate it means that there are no elections, therefore there should be more, and the people should choose the one that they need," Maskhadov said.
Maskhadov proved himself a master tactician in leading his fighters, armed with little more than grenade launchers and automatic rifles, against the might of the Russian army.

His rebels beleaguered the Russian army with inventive, relentless guerrilla attacks which often seemed to come from nowhere and never let Moscow's troops gain a real grip over most of the Moslem region of one million.
Yet he has shown more than just an aptitude for making war.

He led peace negotiations with Moscow that culminated in the signing of a series of agreements earlier this year that formally kept Chechnya in Russia for the next five years while Moscow troops are pulled out of the oil-rich land.

He is widely seen as the most cool-headed among all separatist leaders in an ancient land where petty disputes among local clans often lead to blood fueds and a gun is seen as a natural extension of a man's arm.
Maskhadov's candidacy will be welcomed by Moscow, who sees him as by far the most pragmatic in the separatist ruling circle and a man with whom it can do business.
